opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it flipped some of my assumptions. For a long time, the default way to build a big network was to lean on dynamic routing protocols. Switches talk to each other, discover the topology, and converge on paths. When a link fails, the protocol reconverges and traffic finds a new way around. That model has served the internet incredibly well, so it's natural to carry it into the data center.

Training clusters are a different beast, though. You have enormous, synchronized collective operations, where thousands of GPUs are all waiting on the slowest flow. A link flapping, or a few seconds of reconvergence, doesn't just slow down one connection. It can stall an entire training step across the whole job. So the question became: do we really want the network fabric making all those decisions on its own, on its own timescale?

What MRC let us do was push a lot of that intelligence to the endpoints. The transport spreads traffic across many paths at once, and the endpoints can see very quickly when a path is degraded or gone and simply stop using it, on the order of microseconds rather than waiting for the control plane to sort itself out. Once you have that, much of what the routing protocol was doing for you becomes less essential. You can keep the fabric much simpler and more static, with more predictable paths, and let the transport layer handle load balancing and failure avoidance.

So my thinking shifted from asking how to make routing converge faster to asking how much routing we actually need in the first place. Simpler switches, fewer moving parts in the control plane, and fewer weird emergent behaviors at scale. That matters a lot when you're trying to keep a gigantic training run healthy for weeks at a time. It's not that routing disappears entirely, but its role gets much smaller, and that's been pretty freeing from an operations and reliability standpoint.

r001.rationale: The response says endpoint path detection makes routing less essential and reduces its role, but it explicitly says routing does not disappear entirely, so it does not communicate that a separate routing protocol is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It describes a simpler, more static fabric and says endpoints can avoid failed paths without waiting for the control plane to reconverge.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it really did flip something for me. I came up in a world where the fabric was supposed to be smart. You tuned ECMP, you fought hash polarization, you layered adaptive routing on top, and every time the cluster got bigger the routing problem got harder and more fragile. The implicit assumption was that the network had to figure out where every packet should go, and the endpoints just had to trust it.

MRC, the multipath reliable connection work, pushed a lot of that intelligence out to the edge. If the NIC can spray a single flow across many paths, track what landed, and reorder or retransmit on its own, then the switches don't need to be clever about placement anymore. They just need to be fast and not drop things for dumb reasons. The thing I underestimated was how much of the "need" for sophisticated routing protocols was really a symptom of flows being pinned to one path. Once you break that pinning, the whole category of elephant-flow collisions, the hot links that stall an all-reduce, mostly evaporates as a problem, because the load-balancing is happening at packet granularity by construction.

What it changed in my thinking is where I look first when something is slow. Before, my instinct was to go into the fabric, look at link utilization, convince myself the routing was doing something wrong. Now I start at the transport and ask whether the endpoints are spraying well and whether the fabric is simply lossless enough to not get in the way. The routing protocol becomes much more of a plumbing concern and much less of a performance lever.

I'd be careful not to overstate it. You still need good topology, you still need sane failure handling, and a fabric that reroutes slowly on a link failure will still hurt you at scale. But the mental model shifted from "the network must be smart" to "the network must be simple and honest, and the endpoints carry the intelligence." For training clusters, where every job is one enormous synchronized conversation, that turned out to be a much better fit.

r001.rationale: The response says the NIC sprays packets across paths and handles tracking, reordering, and retransmission, but does not say MRC identifies working paths or makes a separate routing protocol unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response favors simpler switches, but does not describe static switch routing or eliminating control-plane convergence; it says slow rerouting after a link failure can still hurt.

astra-6.text:
The shift for me was separating the need to route traffic from the need for a traditional routing protocol. You still need to get packets to the right destination and keep making progress when something fails. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the network has to discover and manage every path in the way a general-purpose network does.

In a large training network, you have much more structure: you control the topology, the endpoints, and the workload. MRC pushed me to ask how much of that complexity could move to the endpoints, where you can make decisions based on whether communication is actually succeeding.

So I wouldn’t take the lesson as “routing doesn’t matter.” It’s that a routing protocol is one way to provide the properties you need, and it’s worth questioning whether it’s the simplest way in this particular environment.

r001.rationale: The response says MRC can shift decisions to endpoints based on whether communication succeeds, but does not clearly state that MRC identifies working network paths or that this makes a separate routing protocol unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It does not mention static switch routing or explain that it eliminates switch control-plane convergence.

sol-6.1.text:
The big shift was thinking about routing as part of the performance of the training system, rather than just a way to establish connectivity. At that scale, you need to keep the whole job making progress, even when links fail or traffic becomes uneven. A network can be connected and still deliver very poor training performance.

That makes the question less “Do we need a routing protocol?” and more “What does routing need to accomplish for this workload?” You need to use the available paths effectively, respond to failures, and avoid leaving one part of the job waiting on the network. And you want to achieve that with as little operational complexity as possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using available paths and responding to failures, but does not say MRC identifies working paths or that this makes a separate routing protocol unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention static switch routing or eliminating switch control-plane convergence.
